lesson.title: Reading a Function's Whole Story from Its Derivatives
lesson.summary: Curve sketching weaves domain, intercepts, symmetry, asymptotes, the first derivative, and the second derivative into a single coherent picture of what a function's graph actually looks like.
lesson.body:
Every tool built up so far, the First Derivative Test for locating and classifying local extrema, and concavity for describing how a curve bends, exists in service of a bigger goal: being able to picture an entire graph accurately without a calculator. Curve sketching is the procedure that assembles those tools into an order that actually works. Roughly: find the domain first, since nothing else makes sense until you know where the function lives; find the intercepts, since they anchor the curve to the axes; check for symmetry, since it can cut the remaining work in half; locate any asymptotes, since they describe the far edges of the picture; use f' to map out where the curve rises and falls and to locate local extrema; then use f'' to map out concavity and inflection points. The last step is simply to combine all of it into one continuous mental (or hand drawn) picture.

Take f(x) = x^4 - 4x^3. The domain is all real numbers, since this is a polynomial. Factoring gives f(x) = x^3(x - 4), so the x-intercepts are at x = 0 (from the repeated factor x^3, an odd multiplicity of 3) and x = 4 (a simple, multiplicity-1 root). The y-intercept is f(0) = 0, the same point as one of the x-intercepts. Checking symmetry, f(-x) = x^4 + 4x^3, which matches neither f(x) nor -f(x), so the graph has no symmetry to exploit. There are no vertical asymptotes, since polynomials are defined everywhere, and no horizontal asymptote either; instead, because the leading term x^4 has a positive coefficient and even degree, f(x) approaches positive infinity as x approaches both positive and negative infinity.

Now bring in the derivative. f'(x) = 4x^3 - 12x^2 = 4x^2(x - 3), which is zero at x = 0 and x = 3. Since x^2 is never negative, the sign of f'(x) is controlled entirely by the factor (x - 3): f'(x) < 0 for all x < 3 except exactly at x = 0 (where it is momentarily zero), and f'(x) > 0 for x > 3. That sign pattern is worth pausing on. At x = 3, f' changes from negative to positive, so the First Derivative Test confirms a local minimum there, with f(3) = 81 - 108 = -27. But at x = 0, f' is negative immediately to the left and negative immediately to the right too. There is no sign change, so despite the horizontal tangent, x = 0 is not a local extremum at all. The curve flattens out momentarily at the origin and then keeps right on falling.

The second derivative explains why that flattening happens. f''(x) = 12x^2 - 24x = 12x(x - 2), which is zero at x = 0 and x = 2. Testing the sign of f'' across those points: f'' > 0 on (-infinity, 0), f'' < 0 on (0, 2), and f'' > 0 on (2, infinity). Concavity switches at both x = 0 and x = 2, so both are genuine inflection points, at (0, 0) and at (2, f(2)) = (2, 16 - 32) = (2, -16). The inflection at x = 0 is precisely why the tangent there is horizontal without being a local extremum: the curve is concave up just before x = 0 and concave down just after, so it eases into a flat spot and then continues descending rather than turning around.

Putting the whole picture together: coming from the upper left, the curve descends steeply, concave up, crosses through the origin while briefly leveling off (an inflection point, not a turning point), continues descending while now concave down, reaches an inflection at (2, -16) where it becomes concave up again, keeps falling to a local minimum at (3, -27), then rises, crossing the x-axis at x = 4 heading upward, and climbs without bound from there. Every feature, the shape of each piece and the transitions between them, follows directly from the sign charts of f' and f''; nothing about the final picture needed to be guessed.
